title: Four-Way Balanced Cut
source: Reported from HackWithInfy (2021 cycle) — reconstructed from the Codeforces blog post 'Infosys Contest Questions' (entry 90569: make three cuts to split an array into four parts and minimise the difference between the largest and smallest part sums). The same task is known as AtCoder ABC102 D 'Equal Cut'. Statement and samples are original.
statement:
A delivery route is a row of `N` stops; stop `i` has a load of `A[i]` parcels (`A[i] ≥ 1`).

You must make **exactly three cuts** to split the row into **four non-empty contiguous parts** and give one part to each of four drivers. Let `P, Q, R, S` be the total loads of the four parts.

Minimise `max(P, Q, R, S) − min(P, Q, R, S)` and print this minimum.
inputFormat:
The first line contains an integer `N`.
The second line contains `N` integers `A[1..N]`.
outputFormat: Print a single integer — the smallest possible difference between the heaviest and the lightest part.

samples.explanation: Cut as `[3] [2] [4] [1 2]`: loads `3, 2, 4, 3` → difference `4 − 2 = 2`. No cut does better.
`[1 2 3 4] [5] [6] [7]` gives loads `10, 5, 6, 7` (difference 5) — but `[1 2 3] [4 5] [6] [7]` gives `6, 9, 6, 7` (difference 3), which is optimal.

hints: Fix the **middle** cut. Then the left half and the right half are independent: each should be split into two parts whose sums are as close as possible.

With prefix sums, the best split point of the left half `A[0..m)` is where the prefix sum gets closest to `pre[m] / 2`. Because all values are positive, this point only moves **right** as `m` moves right.
So use two pointers (one for the left half, one for the right half) that only advance, giving `O(N)` overall. Evaluate `max − min` of the four sums for each middle cut.
editorial:
### Intuition
Three cuts give `O(N³)` choices. Fix the middle cut at position `m` (left half `A[0..m)`, right half `A[m..N)`). Claim: it is optimal to split each half as evenly as possible.

Why? For the left half with total `X`, splitting into `(p, X − p)` with `p` closest to `X/2` simultaneously **minimises the larger** and **maximises the smaller** of the two parts. The same holds on the right. Since `max(P,Q,R,S) − min(P,Q,R,S)` only depends on the overall max and min, making each half as balanced as possible can never hurt.

### Approach
1. Prefix sums `pre`.
2. Pointer `i` (first cut, `1 ≤ i < m`): advance while `|pre[m] − 2·pre[i+1]| ≤ |pre[m] − 2·pre[i]|`.
3. Pointer `j` (third cut, `m < j < N`): advance while `|total + pre[m] − 2·pre[j+1]| ≤ |total + pre[m] − 2·pre[j]|` (the right half's midpoint is at prefix value `(pre[m] + total)/2`).
4. Since `A[i] ≥ 1`, prefix sums are strictly increasing, so both optimal positions are monotone in `m` — the pointers never move back.
5. Answer = min over `m` of `max − min` of `pre[i], pre[m]−pre[i], pre[j]−pre[m], total−pre[j]`.

### Complexity
`O(N)` time after the prefix sums, `O(N)` memory. (Binary search per middle cut, `O(N log N)`, is also fine.)

### Common mistakes
- Letting a part become empty — keep `i < m < j < N` and `i ≥ 1`.
- Choosing the first cut greedily without considering the closest point on **both** sides of the midpoint (use the `≤` comparison so the pointer moves to the closer position).
- Overflow is not an issue in Python, but sums reach `2·10^14`, so don't use floats.
